column1: # Which Greek verses each verse of the Ge'ez books the church divides its own way answers.
# No source states this. It was worked out in September 2026 by Claude, a language model, reading every
# Ge'ez verse against the Greek: Brenton for Esther, Wisdom and the Letter of Jeremiah, Swete for Proverbs,
# whose rows the frame places as the Hebrew's. A proposal by verse length and a small word table came first;
# each line was then read and kept, moved or merged. Confidence 0.9 where the two plainly say the same,
# less where the church divides a passage differently and the line joins the whole of it.
# Ge'ez book
# The Letter of Jeremiah: the church's text is a shorter letter of 43 verses, read against Brenton's 73.
# Esther: the church's text is the Greek with its additions in place, in thirteen chapters of its own.
# The frame gathers each addition at the verse it follows, so a whole addition answers one row.
# Wisdom: Dillmann's text in 321 longer verses, read against Brenton's 436.
# Messale and Tagsas: the church's two books of Proverbs, in the Septuagint's order, read against Swete's Greek, which the frame places at the Hebrew rows where Brenton gathers 30:1-14 at 24:22.
# Job, the Psalter and the Song of Songs were read in October 2026 by gpt-6.1-sol, a language model of OpenAI,
# through Codex, one chapter at a time against Brenton's Greek as GRCBRENT holds it; every line below 0.9, every
# line with no Greek and a tenth of the rest were read again by Claude, a language model of Anthropic, and the
# few it disputed were settled by reading the verses. The run, its prompts and both readings are kept in
# Resources/Essenthos/generation/geez-wisdom-2026-10-07. The Greek is written here as the rows the frame places
# Brenton's verses at: his plus-verses stand at their verse's row, and his Psalm 115:4a, which the map calls
# Job: the church's text, read against Brenton's.
# The Psalter: Ludolf's, which gives a psalm's title and first verse as one and divides others, read against Brenton's.
# The Song of Songs: the church's text, read against Brenton's.
